title: Trump says triumphal arch will be military complex
description: Trump says triumphal arch will be military complex with drones and snipersFigure caption, A look at the design plans for Trump's triumphal arch as pro
body: Trump says triumphal arch will be military complex with drones and snipersFigure caption, A look at the design plans for Trump's triumphal arch as proposed in AprilByGrace Eliza GoodwinUS President Donald Trump has said his proposed triumphal arch will double as a complex to store military equipment, complete with the ability to deploy snipers and drones.In a Sunday morning post, Trump said he is updating the plans at the "strong request" of the US military and for "national security purposes".The "top grade" military complex and arch will "house, store, and have the rapid ability to use large numbers of drones, plus Snipers, on both the roof and plaza areas, and additionally have and hold large quantities of sniper ammunition in storage", he said.He did not provide details on construction plans or timing, and it's not clear if he needs further approval for the facility.Image source, Getty Images"There will be no facility like this anywhere in the World," Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform. He added that out of "the 59 top cities and Capitals", Washington DC is "the only one in the world that does not have a triumphal arch", without specifying what those cities are. Construction on Trump's 250-foot arch, planned for a site across the Potomac River from Washington DC just outside the Arlington National Cemetery, was expected to begin this month. A rendering of the design from earlier this year includes a golden, winged Lady Liberty on the top of the arch, flanked by two gold eagles, and with the phrases "One Nation Under God" and "Liberty and Justice for All" inscribed in gold on either side of the structure. It will stand 250-feet (76m) from its base to the top of the golden lady statue.At that height, the structure would dwarf the 99-foot Lincoln Memorial nearby and be half as high as the Washington Monument.Image caption, Plans for the arch from earlier this year feature a golden, winged Lady Liberty on the top, flanked by two gold eagles.The Department of Defence declined to provide additional details when reached for comment.Trump has pursued a number of construction projects during his second term to revamp the US capital, including a gilded makeover of the Oval Office, constructing a White House ballroom estimated to cost around $400m, paving over the White House Rose Garden, and renovating the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool.The triumphal arch is one of the biggest projects Trump has set his sights on.

schema.headline: Trump says triumphal arch will be military complex

title: Union calls for halt to graded Ofsted inspections over health concerns
description: England's biggest school leaders' union has called for a halt to graded Ofsted inspections, saying they could pose a "risk to life" for school staff.T
body: England's biggest school leaders' union has called for a halt to graded Ofsted inspections, saying they could pose a "risk to life" for school staff.The National Association of Head Teachers (NAHT) said the change to inspections, rolled out nationally just under a year ago, had been severely harmful to school leaders' welfare.It said schools should instead be rated using short narrative reports that set out their strengths and areas they could improve.Ofsted said it had worked closely with unions and parents to develop the new report card inspection system, and would continue to grade schools.Ofsted, England's schools' inspectorate, introduced the report card system to replace its previous one or two-word judgements last November, following the death of head teacher Ruth Perry, who took her own life after Ofsted downgraded her school from "outstanding" to "inadequate".An inquest ruled that an Ofsted inspection had contributed to her death in January 2023.That led to a change in how Ofsted assessed schools, bringing in report cards designed to grade schools on several areas, rather than focusing on one overall grade for the whole school.But the new system faced criticism from when it was first proposed, with Perry's sister, Prof Julia Waters, saying it appeared to be "a rehash of the discredited and dangerous system it is meant to replace".The NAHT issued a claim with the High Court for a judicial review over the changes, arguing there had not been adequate consultation on the new report cards before they were introduced, but that was rejected.Nearly a year after it was fully rolled out, the NAHT says evidence from its members suggests the new system is having a detrimental impact on school leaders' mental health.Testimonies seen by the BBC suggest head teachers are being left "overwhelmed" and "anxious", with the pressure caused by the inspections described as "intolerable".Although the system had been changed with the intention of lowering the burden on school leaders, the testimonies say the inspection and assessment process had become "higher stakes than ever before".Amanda Hulme, head teacher at Claypool Primary School in Bolton, said a recent inspection at her school had been "easily the most stressful experience" of her career."It was definitely damaging to my health and really quite distressing," she said."I couldn't sleep and it led to my blood pressure and pulse rate increasing."The effect on my team has also been significant, with some colleagues no longer wanting to pursue headship, and another teacher considering leaving the profession entirely."The NAHT says it has shared examples with Education Secretary Lucy Powell of some of the "damaging experiences" it says its members have faced.Speaking to LBC earlier this month, Powell said she took head teacher wellbeing "incredibly seriously" and that the system of accountability needed to be "supportive and understanding."I'll continue the work that I do with head teachers, head teacher representatives and others to make sure that we get this Ofsted framework, but also the culture and the whole regime, right," she added.The NAHT said the results of a recent survey of its members suggested that the majority who responded felt that inspections had worsened in the past 12 months.The union is now calling for inspections to pause to allow for a "fundamental review of how inspection works", drawing on examples from other nations.In Wales, the inspectorate Estyn has removed judgements such as "excellent" and "good" from its reports, instead summarising findings by highlighting a school's strengths and areas for improvement.Northern Ireland's Education and Training Inspectorate (ETI) also uses narrative reports without grades. Scotland's His Majesty's Inspectorate of Education (HIME) does use grades, but there has been a recent consultation on their use.NAHT general secretary Paul Whiteman said: "The clear theme emerging across all the feedback we have received is that this Ofsted framework is even more stressful than the one that preceded it."It poses a real and present danger to the well-being and mental health of school leaders and teachers, possibly even a risk to life."He said he welcomed the new education secretary's focus on teacher wellbeing, adding: "Really fundamental changes to inspection are needed, and we stand ready to work with the new government to achieve that."Responding, Ofsted said it has worked closely with teaching unions over the past three years, to deliver significant reforms and reduce unnecessary pressure on teachers."Ofsted exists to raise standards for children and to provide clear reporting to parents," a spokesperson said."We will continue to engage closely with trades unions – but we will also continue to grade schools."

schema.headline: Union calls for halt to graded Ofsted inspections over health concerns

title: Kelsey Parker welcomes baby after 'devastating' stillbirth
description: Kelsey Parker, the widow of The Wanted singer Tom Parker, has welcomed a baby after last year announcing a "devastating" stillbirth.The podcaster and
body: Kelsey Parker, the widow of The Wanted singer Tom Parker, has welcomed a baby after last year announcing a "devastating" stillbirth.The podcaster and author, 35, had two children with British boy band star Tom Parker before he died in 2022, aged 33, after being diagnosed with terminal brain cancer.She is now in a relationship with Will Lindsay and last June revealed the "earth-shattering news" that they had lost their baby Phoenix.On Sunday, a post on her Instagram account showed a photo of a newborn baby's arm next to a pink sign with the word River. "Welcome to the world, River. Our little bit of hope," the caption said.Celebrities including The Saturdays singer Rochelle Humes, TV presenter Susanna Reid and reality TV star Holly Hagan-Blyth have congratulated Kelsey Parker on social media."Congratulations angel," Rochelle Humes wrote. "Oh my goodness – this is so wonderful – welcome River," Susanna Reid said.Hagan-Blyth commented "I am SO happy for you xxxx".Kelsey Parker's Instagram bio says "turning life's hardest moments into hope".Last year she posted a poem online after the loss of her stillborn baby.It was called Born Sleeping, Forever Loved, and began "the world grew quiet as you arrived, So loved, so longed for, yet not alive. Our precious boy, our angel light, Born with wings, took silent flight".

schema.headline: Kelsey Parker welcomes baby after 'devastating' stillbirth

title: German state elections: Chancellor Friedrich Merz vows to stay on despite 'disaster' in polls
description: Embattled German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has vowed to stay on despite exit polls in two local elections suggesting damaging defeats for his centre-r
body: Embattled German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has vowed to stay on despite exit polls in two local elections suggesting damaging defeats for his centre-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU) party.In the north-eastern state of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, the party was initially projected to scrape through with its worst ever election result. But a few hours later, it dipped below the 5% threshold needed to stay in parliament. Merz called it "a disaster" for his party.Meanwhile the far-right AfD was on track to win the most votes in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, but it is unlikely to govern as other parties refuse to work with it.In Berlin, the ruling CDU was expected to be beaten by Die Linke (The Left).Merz is under mounting pressure, with poor approval ratings and rumours he could even be replaced mid-term in a so-called chancellor swap.Votes took place on Sunday, a fortnight after the CDU saw its vote halved as the Alternative for Germany (AfD) won a major victory in the state of Saxony-Anhalt.Echoing comments he made after that defeat, Merz told reporters at the party's Berlin headquarters on Sunday that he would forge ahead with his coalition government's plans to push through a package of economic, tax and welfare reforms."The reforms have to come," he insisted. "I am taking on this responsibility, because I want to move our country forward"."What needs to be done now requires backbone, steadfastness and patience," Merz said. "I will demonstrate this as CDU party chairman and, above all, as chancellor of our country.""I would even go so far as to say that these reforms are the antidote to the authoritarian poison that, with the fascination of authoritarianism, is penetrating ever deeper into our society," Merz added.The AfD's national co-leader Alice Weidel said: "We are the strongest force and have reached the mainstream of the population."Some branches of the populist AfD are classed as right-wing extremist by domestic intelligence, a designation it strongly rejects.But its anti-immigration, German-first, and Russian-friendly agenda has found fertile ground in the country's former communist east.As the projected results came up on the screen at the CDU's election night gathering in Berlin, there were no cheers or celebration.This is a party that knows it's in trouble, and its leader quickly went on the offensive, declaring that he is going nowhere.Merz has long coveted the top job in German politics, and likely won't give it up easily.Polls for both states closed at 18:00 local time (17:00 BST), with a final result expected later on Sunday night, or even Monday morning.Public broadcasters ZDF and ARD put the AfD slightly ahead in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern. The party was projected to take 38% of the vote share in the state, followed in second place by the centre-left SPD, on 36%.For Berlin, the broadcasters put the CDU on 20% of the vote share when polls closed, behind Die Linke - which has never topped polls in the capital before - on nearly 26%.The AfD also looks set to increase its vote in Berlin, with a projected 16% of the vote.Prior to Sunday's elections, there had been intense speculation in Germany that Merz could be replaced unless his party's political fortunes improved.Earlier this week, the leaders of eight German states backed Merz, who has only been chancellor for 16 months.On Sunday, Burkard Dregger from the CDU in Berlin, told the BBC it was right that Merz should stay on. "He has a lot of work to do and we don't have time to waste to form new government in the federal level".

schema.headline: German state elections: Chancellor Friedrich Merz vows to stay on despite 'disaster' in polls

title: Ed Davey calls for immediate 10p cut to fuel duty
description: Sir Ed Davey is calling on the government to immediately cut fuel duty by 10p a litre until Christmas as part of a package of policies aimed at cuttin
body: Sir Ed Davey is calling on the government to immediately cut fuel duty by 10p a litre until Christmas as part of a package of policies aimed at cutting the cost of living.The Liberal Democrat leader is also urging the government to scrap a permanent increase in fuel duty which is set to take effect in January.Fuel duty was frozen under the Conservatives in March 2022 and Sir Keir Starmer's government continued the freeze, deciding in May to push back a planned 3p increase in September until the end of this year.The Lib Dems claim cutting 10p from fuel duty now would mean fuel would drop by 12p per litre at the pump.Sir Ed claimed drivers should be supported and a temporary three-month fuel duty cut would pay for itself by stimulating the economy."Petrol and diesel prices are higher than they've been for a long time because of Trump's mad war with Iran, and people need help now," he said. The policy would cost about £2bn, he said, adding: "It's a three-month package, a temporary package, but if you look at the extra money the government will get through the energy profits levy, from gas taxes, from VAT and fuel duty, it's self-funding."In a speech to his party's conference on Tuesday, Sir Ed will make further calls to cut the bus fare cap from £3 to £1, and reduce rail fares by 10%.He will also call for VAT to be dropped from public charging points for electric vehicles and a review of network costs the Lib Dems have labelled unfair. Chancellor John Healey is under pressure to raise taxes or cut spending at his Budget next month, amid soaring government borrowing costs.Asked about Sir Ed's call for a fuel duty cut, Labour Party chair Bridget Phillipson told Laura Kuenssberg: "I'm sure John Healey will be open to any and all suggestions ahead of the budget but actually this is an area where the Labour government has taken action on fuel duty already."Whilst I recognise what the Lib Dems have to say on this topic, this is the element of politics about it - they've got their conference, they're making their pitch, good luck to them."Sir Ed also ruled out scrapping the state pension triple lock after party grandee and former business secretary Sir Vince Cable said at a fringe event it was unsustainable and should be "phased out".Speaking at Q&A on the conference stage, Sir Ed said the policy had been introduced by the Lib Dems during the Conservative coalition to address inequalities and there was still work to do to tackle pensioner poverty."It has not finished the job," he told party members, who were split in a show of hands about whether the triple lock should be scrapped if the Lib Dems win power.The triple lock guarantees that the state pension goes up each year in line with either inflation, wage increases or 2.5% - whichever is the highest - but critics say it is unaffordable and unfair to younger people.

schema.headline: Ed Davey calls for immediate 10p cut to fuel duty

title: Man Utd: Michael Carrick defends players after Gary Neville comments
description: Gary Neville took a deep breath after Lisandro Martinez's own goal put Fulham ahead just over an hour into what had been a laboured Manchester United
body: Gary Neville took a deep breath after Lisandro Martinez's own goal put Fulham ahead just over an hour into what had been a laboured Manchester United performance, and delivered his verdict.The former United skipper is never short of a scathing word, but even by his standards, this was brutal."I've watched Manchester United since the age of five and that's the worst 15 minutes I've ever seen," he said. "Absolutely pathetic."I've never seen such a lack of effort. What must [Michael] Carrick be thinking?"For context, Neville was part of the United side beaten 3-1 by Sunday's opponents Fulham at Old Trafford in October 2003. In recent memory they have also lost 7-0 at Liverpool and 6-1 at home twice, to Tottenham and Manchester City.Neville's words came after a poor quarter of an hour from the start of the second half to Martinez's moment of ill fortune, before United went on to snatch a 1-1 draw thanks to Matheus Cunha's deflected strike in the 89th minute.It seemed an extreme reaction. But in a week when United lost the Manchester derby to a City side reduced to 10 men midway through the first half, then against Brighton for the first time in more than 50 years were beaten at home after giving away a two-goal lead, frustration among the fanbase is high.Questions over fitness were first raised during pre-season when midfielder Youri Tielemans revealed United were not prioritising running.While Cunha did not exactly agree with Neville in his post-match interview with Sky Sports, his comments will have fuelled more debate around the issue."At the beginning of the second half they put in more energy than us," said the Brazilian. "We cannot accept this."Unsurprisingly, Carrick had a different take. He used the way his side tried to pressure the home team in the latter stages, leading to Cunha's equaliser, as evidence his squad is fit enough."The way we finished the game, actually, it didn't look like that. We finished the game really strong actually, and kept pushing. I don't think that's an issue, no," he said.Cunha also mentioned the "noise" around United when he spoke to BBC Match of the Day.Neville is a significant part of that noise, either directly or through his growing media empire.Carrick has previously said he can shut it out.It cannot be quite so easy though when United fans - who usually back their team through disappointment - followed up chants on Wednesday in disgust at the Brighton debacle by here booing Carrick's decision to take off popular England midfielder Kobbie Mainoo 11 minutes from time."There's always going to be certain reactions when you're making changes," said Carrick. "I've spoken to Kobbie after the game and he's absolutely fine."I understand at times when we are chasing the game, everyone's a little bit emotional. The supporters are, as well they should be, desperate for us to do the right thing."But I don't take any negatives or offence to it. I think we've just got to try and keep doing the right things to get back into the game."The supporters were unbelievable today, I have to say, all the way through, and stuck with the boys and supported them. At least we've given them something small at the end to take from it, and I'm sure there's more to come."And that is the key point.A draw at Fulham is "something small" considering the home side started the game at the foot of the Premier League - and have now swapped places with Tottenham.Five points from five games leaves United 12th, an incredible 10 points behind pacesetters Manchester City already.Their £70m summer signing Carlos Baleba is still to make his debut, and long-term injury victim Matthijs de Ligt was not involved at all, even though both were part of the squad that travelled south on Saturday.Striker Benjamin Sesko also missed the game after suffering a recurrence of the shin problem against Brighton that he was troubled by for an extended period last season before submitting to a recovery programme that ruled him out for more than three months.Carrick says "at this point" the extent of the damage is unknown.This would all be pretty underwhelming were it not for the ticketing issues instigated by the club's touting crackdown that has annoyed so many in the fanbase.On Wednesday, United will release their full-year financial results to 30 June, around which the full extent of their current debt will be revealed.Then there is the general debate about the wisdom of new stadium, which is set to cost in excess of £2bn, with planning permission potentially submitted with the main Old Trafford masterplan, which is earmarked for late 2027 or early 2028.Little wonder, after leading United back to the Champions League so unexpectedly last season, Carrick is presiding over a club whose supporters feel deflated, even if he does not recognise that."It's still a big season ahead," he said. "It's a long season and you're going to have spells through a season. That's part of the journey."It's not a sprint, it's a long effort."I'm not playing it down, you know. We wanted more points, so I'm not saying everything's great. I understand the frustration. We wanted to be better and we wanted to do other things."But deflation is certainly not what we have within the club and within the group. The players didn't have that on the pitch today and that's what will carry us through the season without a doubt."

schema.headline: Man Utd: Michael Carrick defends players after Gary Neville comments

title: Southampton man rearrested after missing mum's remains found
description: Image source, Police handoutImage caption, Joanne Sheen was reported missing by her family in February 2020ByCurtis LancasterSouth of EnglandA 56-year
body: Image source, Police handoutImage caption, Joanne Sheen was reported missing by her family in February 2020ByCurtis LancasterSouth of EnglandA 56-year-old man has been rearrested on suspicion of conspiracy to commit murder and further arrested on suspicion of murder after human remains were identified as a missing mother-of-three.Joanne Sheen, then aged 44, was last seen when she travelled from Fareham to Southampton with a friend on 5 December 2019.Metropolitan Police officers were called to Padstow Walk in Feltham, London, on 12 August after bones were found in shrubland damaged by a fire a week earlier.The man, from Southampton, first arrested in 2020, has been released on conditional bail. Another man, also 56 and from Southampton, was released on bail after being arrested on suspicion of conspiracy to commit murder.Image source, PA MediaImage caption, The human remains were found at Padstow Walk in Feltham, south-west LondonSheen's disappearance sparked a major police investigation, which the force said led to more than 4,000 lines of inquiry, more than 300 statements taken and searches of more than 10 addresses and numerous water vessels. Sheen was reported missing by her family in February 2020, two months after she was last seen.An investigation led to a number of arrests on suspicion of conspiracy to murder in 2020, but no-one was charged and the case remained unsolved.Officers previously said she had no fixed address and did not own a vehicle or hold a bank account.Image source, PA MediaImage caption, The area damaged by the fire was cordoned off after the remains were found by a member of the publicLondon Fire Brigade attended a fire at Bedfont Pits on 5 August that damaged about two hectares of shrubland.The Metropolitan Police said human remains were found by a member of the public at the site near Bedfont Lakes Country Park a week later. Detectives in London handed the investigation over to Hampshire Police after the remains were identified as those of Sheen.

schema.headline: Southampton man rearrested after missing mum's remains found

title: Laura Kuenssberg: I asked Earl Spencer who we should believe, him or the King?
description: Image caption, Laura Kuenssberg met Earl Spencer at Althorp, the ancestral home on the grounds of which Diana is buriedByPolitical editorWhen I arrive
body: Image caption, Laura Kuenssberg met Earl Spencer at Althorp, the ancestral home on the grounds of which Diana is buriedByPolitical editorWhen I arrived at Althorp on Thursday to speak to Charles, Earl Spencer, only a handful of people were in evidence in the vast stately home, where Princess Diana had once tapdanced in the hall and rollerskated in the cavernous library.It was only hours after Buckingham Palace had sent out its blistering statement in response to the explosive claims made in a new book by Earl Spencer. From the particularly English peace of this grand countryside setting, Diana's brother had provoked a storm.That Palace statement, questioning Earl Spencer's account of the days after his sister's death, was a total contrast to its normal "never explain, never complain" mantra. But it meant that as we sat down, with oil paintings of Earl Spencer's aristocratic ancestors staring down at our TV lights, the interview was not just about his recollections of his sister. It had become about whether the earl, or the King himself, was telling the truth. As we asked Earl Spencer: which Charles are we meant to believe?Figure caption, 'There was a lightness in his tone', says Earl Spencer about Charles' reaction to Diana's deathThat's why it was so important to test Earl Spencer's claims. Was he really sure that the then-Prince Charles had sounded "giddy" after his former wife had died on that terrible night in 1997? Both men, after all, were in a moment of profound shock.Did the earl, a historian and former journalist himself, have evidence of another of his memories, that Charles had "hissed" at him that the world would "forget her soon enough"? Why does he, the uncle of William and Harry, think the world needs to hear his version of events from all those years ago?Earl Spencer was resolute; strong in his conviction that his version of events needed to be told as a matter of record. And he recounted his memories of his conversations with the King in meticulous detail, noting carefully in our discussion that the Palace had not explicitly denied his claims, instead choosing to question his judgement.There is deep unhappiness and frustration in Buckingham Palace at what Earl Spencer has put into the public domain. Their strongly worded statement tells you everything you need to know about how upset they are. "While we do not comment on books as a matter of principle, His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss," it said.Bear in mind that the two Charleses have had a difficult relationship for decades. Even before either of them was born, the Spencers and the Windsors, two aristocratic families, had years of splits and spats. In the past 48 hours, allies on either side have lined up to back the two different accounts, with acolytes of the King suggesting he would never have said such things. Others emerged to back Spencer.There is no way of being completely sure what exactly happened. There hasn't been an explicit denial, but the Palace has objected in very strong terms to how Earl Spencer has presented the past. But speaking to Diana's brother for about half an hour, I felt he seemed entirely sure in his own mind. His book is carefully constructed to give his account, as well as pay tribute to his sister's life as the 30th anniversary of her death approaches.Princess Diana: My Sister's StoryWatch the full interview with Laura Kuenssberg.After we had spoken, we walked down to the lake on the estate where, on a wooded island, Diana was laid to rest. It's a place where, Earl Spencer told me, she could be safe from intrusion, and is marked as a burial place with a huge stone urn.We passed the little green rowing boat he uses to go to the island to visit her, and walked to what he calls The Temple. It's an 18th Century building that now bears her name and includes a quote from her and another from his famous eulogy to her. It's a line he now says was specifically intended to be a riposte to the other Charles' suggestion that she would quickly be forgotten: Diana "will never be extinguished from our minds".Earl Spencer told me he was not being "vengeful" and that he was not trying to damage the monarchy - even saying there was more he knew about the King that he could relate but had chosen not to. But by speaking out so boldly, publishing his book, serialising it in the papers, and speaking to us, the earl was not just paying a moving tribute to his sister, but stirring up the long-running contest for control of Diana's memory.Figure caption, Watch: 'You never get over it': Earl Spencer's emotional tribute to late sister DianaIn the closing moments of our interview, Earl Spencer revealed himself not to be a public figure trying to settle old scores or correct myths about his incredibly famous sister. When I asked how much he missed her, he welled up, and nearly three decades on, the tears still came. He said he missed her every day. "The thing with sibling loss? You never get over it," he said.Charles Spencer was a young man when his sister died at 36 in the most awful circumstances. He joked about crying as a 62-year-old man at the end of a TV interview in which he'd discussed the monarchy and also made claims about the King that he was well aware would stir up controversy around the world. In the normally hidden world of Althorp, the grief of a brother was still plainly on display – what happened to Princess Diana is not all in the past.

schema.headline: Laura Kuenssberg: I asked Earl Spencer who we should believe, him or the King?

title: Danny Dyer among celebrities at water public ownership protest
description: Actor Danny Dyer, his daughter Dani Dyer and singer Becky Hill have attended a protest in Kent demanding public ownership of the water industry.Activi
body: Actor Danny Dyer, his daughter Dani Dyer and singer Becky Hill have attended a protest in Kent demanding public ownership of the water industry.Activists from Surfers Against Sewage descended on Leysdown on Sunday after 315,000 signed a petition calling for the water industry to be returned to public ownership.Rivals and EastEnders star Dyer, who has been running a caravan park on Isle of Sheppey as part of a new TV series, told the BBC: "Sometimes when you look out to the sea, you can smell the twang in the air."Water UK said that "no sewage spill is ever acceptable", while Southern Water said it was committed to reducing storm overflows.Dyer said that the quality of the water was "a disgrace"."It's a very dangerous thing," he told the BBC.Meanwhile Hill said that she loved swimming in the open water but found it "disgusting" to find human waste in the sea.She said that she was campaigning for her family and other families for a cleaner sea."We can stand up and make a difference," she added.Meanwhile Cliff Roney, a GMB activist who has worked in the water industry for more than 40 years, said: "I have seen this industry at its very best and now at its very worst."If the industry is not brought back into public ownership quickly, we are heading towards a national catastrophe."Water UK said it was working to end sewage spills "as fast as we physically can"."That's why we are tripling investment over the next five years to halve spills from storm overflows and upgrade the capacity of 1,700 wastewater treatment works," a spokesperson said."This is part of a record £104bn investment programme – the largest in the industry's history – to stop sewage entering our rivers and seas, secure our water supplies and support economic growth."Southern Water's director for environment and innovation, Nick Mills, said its 10-year, £1.5bn Clean Rivers and Seas Plan was "already starting to make a difference"."In Whitstable, we're harnessing both AI and nature-based solutions, and we're investing £90m in improvements to Swalecliffe Wastewater Treatment Works. Together, these measures will dramatically reduce storm overflows in the area."According to Defra's Bathing Water Quality site, the most recent classification for Leysdown is rated good, based on samples taken from 2022 to 2025.There have been no pollution incidents reported there, the website states. Follow BBC Kent on Facebook, external, on X, external, on Instagram, external and listen to BBC Radio Kent on Sounds. Send your story ideas to southeasttoday@bbc.co.uk, external or WhatsApp us on 08081 002250.

title: Richard Hammond thanks 999 crews on Elvington crash anniversary
description: Former Top Gear presenter Richard Hammond has thanked emergency services for their help on the 20th anniversary of the crash in which he was nearly ki
body: Former Top Gear presenter Richard Hammond has thanked emergency services for their help on the 20th anniversary of the crash in which he was nearly killed.Hammond was seriously injured in September 2006 when the 320mph (515km/h) jet-powered Vampire dragster he was driving veered off the track at Elvington airfield, near York, during filming for the BBC show.In an Instagram post, Hammond said he wanted to thank the members of the staff who rescued him and supported him following the accident "from the bottom of my heart".In the post, he spoke of the events of that day and said he would be "forever grateful" to all those who helped him in the aftermath of the crash.He wrote: "Twenty years ago today, I came to an abrupt stop upside down in a Yorkshire field, convinced I was about to die."He said he recalled having pulled the lever to release the car's parachute before trying to steer it away from disaster, "but disaster was, it seemed, my fate"."Having done everything I could to avert it, I gave myself over to that fate," he said.

schema.headline: Richard Hammond thanks 999 crews on Elvington crash anniversary

title: What we have learned from the Premier League so far as international break looms
description: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Brighton's 3-0 win over Arsenal could have a big impact on both teams' seasonsByEmlyn BegleyBBC Sport journal
body: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Brighton's 3-0 win over Arsenal could have a big impact on both teams' seasonsByEmlyn BegleyBBC Sport journalistThe Premier League takes a near three-week break as we enter a four-game international window.So, what have we learned from the opening five matches of the season? BBC Sport takes a look.Arsenal are beatableFigure caption, Highlights: Brilliant Brighton batter Arsenal in shock first defeat as championsPremier League champions Arsenal were looking fairly unstoppable in the opening weeks of the season.A win over Brighton on Saturday would have given the Gunners a club-record equalling eighth consecutive win in all competitions to start the season. But that all ended with a 3-0 loss at Amex Stadium on Saturday.The Gunners had not lost a league game by more than one goal, let alone three, since October 2024. It was their heaviest defeat in the league since May 2023 when they lost 3-0 to the same opposition."That's not going to take away what the team has done and the boys have done in the last six or seven weeks since coming back from the World Cup," said boss Mikel Arteta."What we've done, the way we've competed and the amount of games we've won has been remarkable - but this is a big lesson for all of us to understand what it takes to win at this level."Maresca hits ground running at Man CityFigure caption, Man City come out on top in eight goal thriller against SunderlandMany wondered if Manchester City would experience a post-Pep Guardiola slump when the legendary boss left after a decade.Things did not start too well under Enzo Maresca, with the Community Shield defeat by Arsenal.But they have won all five games in the Premier League - and seven in a row in all competitions - after Sunday's entertaining 5-3 win over Sunderland.That takes them three points clear of Arsenal."In the press conference before the game, I said I expect a very tough game," said Maresca. "Then we also conceded two or three goals but we have learned a lot in these eight weeks and this is good."Brighton & Brentford continue to impressFigure caption, Brentford stay unbeaten as they put three past ChelseaBrighton and Brentford, two clubs who have never won a major trophy, have continued to impress this season.Fabian Hurzeler's Brighton enjoyed that 3-0 win over Arsenal to see them sit third in the table, only two points behind the Gunners.Brighton have won at home against the reigning Premier League champions in each of the last three seasons.Star player Pascal Gross laughed and said "no" when BBC Sport asked him if Albion were in the title race. But stranger things have happened...Meanwhile, just one point below them in the table are Keith Andrews' Brentford.Many tipped the Bees to struggle after the departure of Thomas Frank last summer but if anything they improved under their former set-piece coach Andrews.And their start to this season - unbeaten after five games and fourth in the table - is showing he is no one-season wonder as a manager.They go into the break on the back of their most impressive result, a 3-0 home win over Chelsea.Leeds, impressing again under boss Daniel Farke, are also on nine points and in a potential Champions League place.Andoni Iraola's Liverpool and Everton are just below them on goal difference.Carrick under pressure?Figure caption, Cunha's late strike denies Fulham first league win of the seasonSeven years apart, United did the same thing twice hoping for different results - appointing a club legend who last managed in Britain in the Championship after a good start as caretaker boss.In 2019 it was Ole Gunnar Solskjaer and this time it was Michael Carrick.But this season, after Carrick having a summer to work on his team, the Red Devils have only won once in the league.Their five points after five league games is their joint fewest at this stage of a Premier League season.They go into the international break on the back of a 1-1 draw against Fulham, and even needed a late deflected Matheus Cunha strike to stop the Cottagers winning their first game all season.After the Lisandro Martinez own goal that give Fulham the lead, ex-United captain Gary Neville said on Sky Sports: "I've watched Manchester United since the age of five and that's the worst 15 minutes I've ever seen. "Absolutely pathetic. I've never seen such a lack of effort."United's owners will have almost three weeks to stew on this before they host fellow underachievers Tottenham (more on them soon) on 10 October.Figure caption, Coventry defeat Forest for first win since Prem returnIn 2024 and 2025, the three promoted teams went straight back down - mostly with really low points tallies too.But that streak came to an end last year when Sunderland finished seventh to qualify for Europe and Leeds came 14th. Only Burnley went down.And the early weeks of this season indicate we could be in for a similar situation.Hull City are eighth after five games, with their 2-1 loss to Newcastle their first defeat.Ipswich are 11th. And Coventry, after losing the first four games without scoring, beat Nottingham Forest 1-0 and only sit in the drop zone on goal difference.No quick fix at SpursFigure caption, Highlights: Villa survive late Spurs scare for first PL win of the seasonTottenham finished 17th the last two seasons, their lowest two finishes since being in the second tier in 1977-78.But expectations were raised after a summer of big spending - with Spurs splashing out £302m as well as making two high-profile loan signings.Defence and midfield in particular were overhauled, with new wingers too.But they are left with one senior striker in Dominic Solanke, who has only scored 12 Premier League goals in over two years at the club."I feel they have overpaid for every player they bought this summer - you can't rule them out from being in and around the relegation battle," said TNT pundit and ex-England international Joe Cole.Saturday's 3-2 loss against Aston Villa sees them sit 19th going into the break - despite scoring their first two league goals of the campaign."We have to put on the pitch something more than we are putting," said manager Roberto de Zerbi."Football is tactical but it is blood, it is fighting, it is first one on the ball. We will suffer until the next game."Chelsea are the great entertainersMany were keen to see what Xabi Alonso could do at Chelsea this season.The Spaniard memorably led Bayer Leverkusen to a historic unbeaten German double in 2023-24.And they made big changes to their squad this summer, with £117m attacking midfielder Morgan Rogers and new first-choice keeper Emiliano Martinez both coming in from Aston Villa.There have been 22 goals in their five league games - more coming against them than for them - and they sit 10th.And that is not even counting the 6-3 win over Leeds in the Carabao Cup.Hugely entertaining for the neutrals - but perhaps not for Chelsea fans or management.

schema.headline: What we have learned from the Premier League so far as international break looms

title: Key takeaways from BBC interview as Earl Spencer defends claims about King
description: ByAndré Rhoden-Paul Earl Spencer has told the BBC writing his book about sister Princess Diana, which has made headlines for its criticism of King Cha
body: ByAndré Rhoden-Paul Earl Spencer has told the BBC writing his book about sister Princess Diana, which has made headlines for its criticism of King Charles, was his "duty...as an eyewitness to history".In an interview with the BBC's Laura Kuenssberg ahead of the memoir's release on Tuesday, Earl Spencer said he wanted "to put things down once and for all that were true".Among claims made in Swan Song about the King, who was then the Prince of Wales, was that he said "we'll forget her soon enough" during an argument over whether Princes William and Harry should walk in Diana's funeral procession.In a strongly worded response, Buckingham Palace said the King was "mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgement and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss".Here are the key moments from Earl Spencer's interview, which include his first account of how he was told about Diana's death and criticism of press coverage of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex. Earl initially told Diana's crash was 'not too serious'Earl Spencer was in South Africa when Princess Diana died in a Paris car crash in the early hours of 31 August 1997, along with close friend Dodi Fayed and the driver of the car.He told the BBC he got a call in the middle of the night from his sister Lady Jane Fellowes, who said Princess Diana had been in a crash but "it's not too serious". But then he "kept getting more and more distressing calls" from his sister. "And then my sister Jane said, 'I'm afraid she's died.' It started... as a little prang, and then it became a broken leg, perhaps a head injury, and then death."Charles had 'giddy tone' after Diana's deathFigure caption, Earl Spencer describes 'giddy tone' in Charles' voice during call after Diana's deathDescribing the hours after her death, Earl Spencer said he took a call at his home in Cape Town from Prince Charles, who told him how he broke the news to Princes William and Harry at Balmoral Castle. "I felt there was a sort of giddy tone," he told the BBC. "I'd had a lot of calls that day from people who cared, who were stunned... and I just felt there was a lightness in his tone about Diana's death that really jarred with me."In his book, Earl Spencer compares his tone to like a "lottery winner" and says he suspects the prince's reaction was based on how this event would free him to marry the woman he loved, his future wife Queen Camilla. When asked by Kuenssberg if he could be sure that is what Prince Charles was thinking, Earl Spencer said: "I cannot be sure, I'm saying that's what I assume from the tone is a possibility." Image caption, Princess Diana: My Sister's Story. The full interview with Laura Kuenssberg is available on BBC iPlayer and will be broadcast on BBC One at 18:30 BST on Sunday Earl Spencer told the BBC he had been discussing funeral arrangements with a palace official, who said it had been agreed Princes William and Harry should walk behind their mother's coffin. Unhappy, he said he told the official it is not what his sister would have wanted, before the conversation came to an end. Soon after, the earl says he took a call from Prince Charles, who asked him about his opposition to it. "I said, 'Well, of course not, sir, she wouldn't want it'. And then he said, 'Well, I walked behind Lord Mountbatten's coffin.' And I said, 'Yes, but you were 30 and he wasn't your mother'."He then claims Charles went "ballistic... and ranted for a while" about the Spencer's sense of duty not being adequate enough before "he said 'We'll forget her [Diana] soon enough'.""I really was so stunned and after a stunned silence I said 'I can not believe you just said that' and I hung up on him", the earl told Kuenssberg during his sit down interview at his Althorp estate. Image source, PA MediaImage caption, Princes William and Harry walked in the procession behind their mother's coffinResponding to the Palace's statement pushing back on the story, Earl Spencer said: "I can tell you here and now, those are exactly the words he said. "I've only ever had two calls on the line with Prince Charles at any stage in my life. "I was hyper-alert to what he was saying, and those are precisely the words he said. And I promise that to you now. Genuinely, that is what he said. "I don't hear him saying he didn't say that."The earl said he told "close friends and family" about the "monstrous" comment. When asked if people should believe him or the King, he said: "Well, I'm telling the truth... what else would have made me hang up on the King that day?"On what Princes William and Harry might think of the comments being brought up nearly 30 years later, he added the words "will not be a surprise" to the brothers.He also said his renowned funeral eulogy, in which he said his sister's qualities would never be "extinguished from our minds", was a "direct rebuttal" of the prince's comments. 'I know lots of things about the King' not in the bookTalking about his motivations for writing the book, Earl Spencer, aged 62, said it was his "duty... as an eyewitness to history" and as someone in the "final season of my life" with his parents dying in their sixties."I'm aware of mortality and I wanted to just put things down once and for all that were true," the historian and journalist explained."This is not a threat, it's a fact, I know lots of things about the King which I chose not to include in the book because they were not relevant."When put to him that the  statement sounded like a threat when it involved potentially damaging information, he said: "No, not at all a threat, it's just the reality."Kuenssberg questioned why he included an account of a conversation in which his sister told him Prince Charles was in love with his valet - a claim Earl Spencer said was improbable - and asked if he was motivated in including some of these allegations to create interest to sell the book. "It's in the context of a conversation where Diana is telling me that her marriage is over," the earl replied."It's a brother's tribute, a loving tribute to a sister.  And I think she deserves honesty so that's what I've delivered."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Earl Spencer said he was concerned about security for Duke and Duchess of SussexEarl Spencer worries about Harry's lack of police protectionWhen asked about how he thinks Prince Harry has been treated by the Royal Family, Earl Spencer told the BBC he is reluctant to discuss it, but he said he was concerned about his security. "I would say that I personally worry about the fifth-in-line to the throne who's served in the military not having any police protection," he said. "As an uncle who's seen his sister die in very, very preventable circumstances, that I would veer towards protection."It is understood the committee that oversees royal and VIP security, known as Ravec, is to reconsider Prince Harry and Meghan's level of police protection now they and their two children are full-time residents in the UK rather than visitors.When asked about how the press treated Princess Diana and now Prince Harry and Meghan, he said tabloid articles "could be really really unpleasant". "It would really be beholden on people to learn from Diana's example. I'm not here to speak for Harry and Meghan, but for anyone who's being destroyed in this way daily, it must be such a cancerous influence in their life," Earl Spencer said. "[Diana] was really brought low by all that criticism. And yeah I suppose it's a pity when I see echoes of that now."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The earl said he hopes his nephews resolve their differences'I hope William and Harry resolve row' Earl Spencer said he did not take sides - as he perceives is the "perception in the media" - in the dispute between Princes William and Harry. "I'm on my deceased sister's sons' side, both of them. And if either of them wanted anything then I'd be equally there for them," he said. "And I never get involved in one camp or the other, except as a benign figure I hope."He said there are a "lot of reasons on both sides" why the brothers' relationship had "got to this stage". "I hope one day it's resolved, but I don't know all – I certainly don't know what's been done in the finer detail and so I would feel intrusive if I got more involved than to say of course a mother would want her two sons to be happy together and love each other," he said. Diana 'convinced she couldn't trust people' after Bashir interviewReflecting on the time before Princess Diana's death, Kuenssberg asked if the infamous BBC Panorama interview with journalist Martin Bashir in 1995 might have been linked indirectly to his sister finding herself in Paris in 1997. Shortly after the interview broadcast, in which Princess Diana admitted having an affair and said Prince Charles's affair with then-Camilla Parker Bowles made her feel worthless, the Queen wrote to Prince Charles and Princess Diana telling them to divorce.A 2021 inquiry found Bashir acted in a "deceitful" way  by mocking up fake bank statements - which falsely suggested individuals were being paid to keep Diana under surveillance - and showing them to Earl Spencer to gain access to the late princess.Earl Spencer said he did make "a connection" between the crash and the Panorama interview and said they conned both him and Diana."People said, 'Oh, she was paranoid'. She wasn't paranoid. She was convinced that she couldn't trust people because the evidence was there.  And, you know, I think that left her vulnerable that night."The BBC and Bashir apologised to King Charles, Earl Spencer and Princes William and Harry after the 2021 report was published.The BBC's then-director general, Tim Davie, said: "Although the report states that Diana, Princess of Wales, was keen on the idea of an interview with the BBC, it is clear that the process for securing the interview fell far short of what audiences have a right to expect. We are very sorry for this."Earl supports 'a modern monarchy'Earl Spencer, the ninth earl of an aristocratic family whose peerage dates back to the 18th Century and retains its vast estate, told the BBC he is "all for a monarchy, but I like a modern monarchy". Talking about the "jarring" protocol around the monarchy, he said: "You know, you mentioned the statement earlier, 'His Majesty says", I just don't think it's healthy for a human being to be seen in such archaic, servile terms."When Kuenssberg asked him if he supported this monarchy, following the damning book he has just written, he said: "I do."He added when challenged: "Well, I'm not dealing with King Charles as monarch in this book, this is all 30-odd years ago and what was said and done then."An emotional tribute to a sister he misses every dayFigure caption, Watch: 'You never get over it': Earl Spencer's emotional tribute to late sister DianaAs the interview came to an end, Earl Spencer was asked whether he would ever be able to get over his sister's death.Visibly emotional, he said he misses Diana "every day", adding "that's the thing with sibling loss, you never get over it."But his upcoming book, he said, is a way for him to have a final say on Diana's life before stepping off "into the sunset"."One of the reasons I called this Swan Song actually is because it's my sign off," he said."I have been Diana's brother, this is my final take on the situation… I'm not here to bang on about Diana, this is my final word, a celebration of her."

schema.headline: Key takeaways from BBC interview as Earl Spencer defends claims about King

title: Will you get £13,000 a year when you stop working? Here's how to check
description: Image source, Getty ImagesByCost of living correspondentIt may well be decades away, but do you know how much money you will get when you stop working
body: Image source, Getty ImagesByCost of living correspondentIt may well be decades away, but do you know how much money you will get when you stop working?The current state pension is soon likely to top £13,000 a year.Yet one in eight people surveyed by the UK tax authority have never checked how much money they are forecast to receive.Here's how to find out, and what you can do now to boost it.How much is the state pension?If you're working, it is highly likely you're contributing to the state pension - paid by the government when you hit pension age in your late 60s. At the moment:the flat-rate state pension - for those who reached state pension age after April 2016 - is £241.30 a week (£12,547.60 a year)the old basic state pension - for those who reached state pension age before April 2016 - is £184.90 a week (£9,614.80 a year)Many people on the old basic state pension may receive a top-up called the additional state pension. Most pensioners have other income, primarily from pension savings built up over their career.The state pension goes up each year in line with the highest of either inflation, wage increases, or 2.5%. So next April, the flat-rate state pension is expected to go above £13,000.How do I qualify for it?Workers pay National Insurance (NI) contributions. In general, you need 35 years of qualifying contributions to get a full state pension.You may have gaps in your NI record if, for example, you have lived abroad. If you've taken time away from work to care for children or family members, then you get NI credits if you receive child benefit or carer's allowance.It's possible to boost your contribution history with voluntary payments. Since April 2025, you have only been able to make payments for the previous six years.That's one reason why it is important to check your state pension forecast well before you retire, experts say.How do I check what I'll get?You can see what you are forecast to receive:By downloading the HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC) app, externalUsing the official online state pension forecast webpage, externalTo get a state pension, you will need to prove your identity using official photo ID.Importantly, never click on a link sent in an unsolicited email or text message, even if it looks official, as it could be a scam.For more general information about tax and pensions, HMRC has launched a Tax Confident website, external.And the government-funded, independent Money Helper website has a free retirement guidance tool, external to walk you through the options.Why haven't you checked?The most common reason for not checking a state pension forecast was feeling that retirement was still too far away to think about, a recent survey of 5,000 consumers by HMRC found.Losing track of pension pots from previous jobs, and concerns about how career breaks might affect their entitlement, were also frequent responses.People aged 45-54 were the most likely to have never checked."Whether retirement is decades away or just around the corner, I'd encourage everyone to check their forecast and see if there's anything they can do now to boost their entitlement later," says Myrtle Lloyd, HMRC's chief customer officer.

schema.headline: Will you get £13,000 a year when you stop working? Here's how to check

title: England and Wales to have specialist courts for rape cases
description: Specialist courts to handle cases of rape and other sexual offences will be introduced across England and Wales over the next two years, the prime min
body: Specialist courts to handle cases of rape and other sexual offences will be introduced across England and Wales over the next two years, the prime minister has announced.Each crown court will have at least one courtroom especially set up to hear such cases, while victims will be able to view proceedings remotely and give evidence from a separate room via video link.Victims will also be provided with private entrances and waiting rooms to separate them from defendants, though it is understood this will be dependent on the architecture of each building.Rape Crisis England and Wales said this was a "significant step forward" and addressed several reforms it had been requesting for many years."Taken together, they reflect the urgency of ensuring that courts are fit for purpose and properly meet the needs of victims and survivors, which is crucial to securing justice," said the charity's chief executive, Ciara Bergman.Under the new measures, expected to cost around £23m from the Ministry of Justice's budget, court staff will be given "trauma-informed training" and a single person of contact will be assigned to each survivor.From next month, trials will be given a fixed date rather than placed on floating lists in what Prime Minister Andy Burnham said was an effort to "rebalance the scales of justice and put victims first".The government said the changes follow Labour MP Charlotte Nichols showing "immense strength and bravery" in speaking publicly about being raped and calling for changes to the justice system.Nichols waived her automatic right to anonymity in March when she made a Commons speech and described having to wait more than 1,000 days to go to court.Earlier this year, the government announced that rape victims would be given access to specialist legal advice throughout the criminal justice process.Labour promised in its 2024 manifesto to halve violence against women and girls within a decade."For too long, victims of rape and serious sexual offences have felt let down by our justice system," Burnham said. "Prosecution rates for rape remain shamefully low, with many victims waiting years for justice. This is not good enough."The changes were "long overdue" and would make a "significant difference" but focusing on prosecution alone would not be enough, he added. "So as well as ensuring victims get justice, we will step up action to prevent these horrific crimes from happening in the first place," the prime minister said.Nichols spoke publicly for the first time about being raped when she accused the then Justice Secretary, David Lammy, of using crime victims as a "cudgel" to push through his reforms of the legal system.She was criticising the Courts and Tribunals Bill's plans to limit jury trials to cases with a likely prison sentence of three years or more.She said she had waited 1,088 days to go to court, with every day being "agony" and the "trauma" made worse by her role in public life.Her attacker, she said, was acquitted at crown court but subsequently ordered to pay compensation after she won a civil case against him."It is because I have been raped that I am as passionate as I am about what it means for a justice system to be truly victim-focused," she said."It is because I have endured every indignity that our broken criminal justice system could mete out that I care what kind of reform will actually deliver justice for survivors and victims of crime more widely."Responding to news of the specialist courts being rolled out, the Conservatives said tackling delays to criminal rape trials was "long overdue" and they pushed Labour to commit to scrapping plans to restrict jury trials. "The fact that victims have been withdrawing their cases because they have taken too long has been a disgrace," said shadow justice secretary Nick Timothy.  "Labour need to get courts sitting throughout the year, end the delays and clear the backlog – not undermine our right to a trial by jury."Last year another charity, the Salford Survivor Project, said victims of rape and sexual assault were being "failed by the system" as court backlogs reached a record high.The long delays for cases to go to trial were having a serious impact on victims' mental health, it said.Also last year, a woman who says she was sexually assaulted by a taxi driver on her 21st birthday told BBC News she had dropped the case because of court delays.She reported the alleged incident in early 2022 and gave evidence in court in December 2023 but the case was adjourned until September 2024 when the judge fell ill."I made the decision, even though I hate the statement, to drop the case," she said. "I couldn't let this hurt me further."The Crown Prosecution Service said that, without her testimony, the case had been dropped because of insufficient evidence.If you have been affected by any of the issues raised in this story, information and support can be found at the BBC's Action Line website.

schema.headline: England and Wales to have specialist courts for rape cases
